result.question: 전자혀(요똥용 한식 조미료 배합 계산기) 앱의 '맛 모델'을 요리과학/감각과학 문헌으로 검증한다. 감칠맛 시너지(MSG:IMP), 맛 혼합 억제(mixture suppression), 짠-신-쓴-단 상호작용, 음식별 적정 염도(% w/w), 산미의 역할, 한식 조미료의 나트륨/감칠맛 정량, 캡사이신(TRPV1)의 별도 처리, 규칙기반 선형+상호작용항 모델로 palatability를 예측하는 것의 타당성을 권위 있는 출처로 교차검증하고 맞음/과단순화/틀림으로 판정하라.
result.summary: 10개 claim은 (a) 미각 상호작용의 정신물리학(시너지·억제·비단조성), (b) 음식·조미료의 정량 데이터(염도, 한식 장류 나트륨/아미노산, 전자혀·메타볼로믹스), (c) 예측 모델의 타당성 3개 축으로 묶인다. 각 축을 1차 문헌(Yamaguchi, Keast & Breslin, Breslin & Beauchamp)과 응용 데이터(전자혀/메타볼로믹스, 식품 염도 가이드라인)로 나눠 검색해 핵심 수치와 한계를 동시에 확보하도록 각도를 배분한다.

results.title: Yamaguchi (1967) — The Synergistic Taste Effect of Monosodium Glutamate and Disodium 5′-Inosinate (J. Food Science)
results.snippet: THE primary source for Claim 1. Establishes the synergy mathematically: equivalent MSG intensity y = u + γ·u·v (γ ≈ 1.218×10⁸ in g/dl² for IMP). Critically, the multiplicative term means synergy peaks near a 1:1 MSG:IMP mass ratio in pure solution and can reach ~7-8x the intensity of either alone AT THAT TOTAL CONCENTRATION — not a fixed 7-8x at all ratios. This nuance is what the app's coefficient must respect: the 7-8x figure is the maximum in dilute pure water, not the typical in-food multiplier.

results.title: Equivalent Umami Concentration (EUC) — Yamaguchi et al. 1971 formula explained
results.snippet: Operationalizes Yamaguchi into the EUC formula (Y = Σaibi + 1218·Σaibi·Σajbj), the standard tool food scientists use to convert real glutamate + IMP/GMP/AMP content into mg-MSG-equivalents. Directly relevant to Claim 8 (quantifying umami vectors of Korean jang/sauces) and to setting a defensible synergy coefficient in the app instead of a flat 7-8x. The 1218 coefficient is the in-practice anchor.

results.title: Umami and Food Palatability (J. Nutrition / ScienceDirect) — Yamaguchi review
results.snippet: Yamaguchi's own review data showing the synergy as a continuous function of the IMP fraction, with maximum equivalent intensity near a ~1:1 (and per some summaries 70:30 IMP-region) mix. Establishes that in actual foods the realized multiplier is far below the 7-8x pure-solution ceiling because background glutamate is already high and nucleotide levels are low — key correction for the app's over-stated synergy claim.

results.title: Time-intensity profiles of flavor potentiators (MSG, IMP, GMP)
results.snippet: Empirical sensory data: mixtures of 10 and 5 mM MSG with 2.5 mM IMP or GMP gave the highest umami intensities, confirming that maximal synergy occurs at moderate, comparable molar levels — not at extreme ratios. Useful for calibrating realistic in-food synergy magnitudes rather than the theoretical 7-8x maximum.

results.title: MSG, IMP, and GMP Flavor Enhancers in Savory Foods (industry application)
results.snippet: Documents the industrial 'sweet spot' (e.g. ~95% MSG + 5% I+G blends) that delivers several-fold umami boosts in real formulations. Shows the gap between the lab-optimal 1:1 synergy and the practical low-nucleotide ratios used in actual seasoning — important for the app to recommend realistic dosing rather than a 1:1 textbook ratio.

results.title: Umami synergy as the scientific principle behind taste-pairing champagne and oysters (Scientific Reports 2020)
results.snippet: Modern application of the Yamaguchi EUC model to real foods (glutamate-rich + IMP-rich pairing), quantifying realized synergy in actual food matrices. Demonstrates how the foundational formula translates to measured multipliers in food context, supporting a corrected, sub-maximal synergy coefficient for the app.

results.title: Suppression of Central Taste Transmission by Oral Capsaicin (Simons et al., J. Neurosci. 2003)
results.snippet: Direct neural evidence for Claim 9 masking: gustatory neuron responses in the nucleus tractus solitarius were depressed to a mean 61.5% of control immediately after oral capsaicin. Establishes that capsaicin (TRPV1/trigeminal) suppresses central taste transmission rather than acting as a taste itself — quantifies a masking coefficient (~38% reduction) the app could use.

results.title: Capsaicin as a probe of the relationship between bitter taste and chemesthesis (Prescott & Stevenson lineage; Physiology & Behavior)
results.snippet: Psychophysical foundation for Claim 9: capsaicin selectively suppresses suprathreshold sweetness, bitterness, and umami (MSG) while leaving salt and SOUR essentially unaffected. Critical nuance for the app — masking is quality-specific and non-uniform, not a flat 'spice reduces all tastes' term. Also shows capsaicin can itself evoke a weak bitter response at circumvallate papillae.

results.title: Interactions between Chemesthesis and Taste: Role of TRPA1 and TRPV1 (Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2021)
results.snippet: Authoritative review grounding Claim 9: capsaicin acts via TRPV1 on trigeminal somatosensory fibers (chemesthesis/pain), NOT the gustatory system, justifying a separate model. Documents bidirectional masking — taste stimuli partially mask burn and capsaicin attenuates tastes — and that integration occurs both peripherally and in the CNS.

results.title: Bliss point (food) — overview of Moskowitz's inverted-U hedonic optima
results.snippet: Core of Claim 10: liking follows an inverted-U with an intermediate optimum (bliss point) for sugar and salt, so more-is-better linear terms fail. Notes synergy from fat/sugar/salt combinations exceeds additive effects (nonlinearity) and that preferences segment across consumers — directly limits a single global linear+interaction palatability model.

results.title: Distinct Sensory Hedonic Functions for Sourness in Adults (PMC 2024)
results.snippet: Empirical support for the individual/cultural-variation limit in Claim 10: adults split into qualitatively DIFFERENT hedonic functions for sourness (some monotonic-up, some inverted-U). No single curve fits the population — a rule-based model with one coefficient set per tastant cannot capture this heterogeneity. Echoes Moskowitz's tamarind-exposure cultural finding.

results.title: Perceptual and Affective Responses to Sampled Capsaicin Differ by Reported Intake (Chem. Senses / PMC 2017)
results.snippet: Reinforces both claims: capsaicin burn intensity and especially its hedonic valence (liking vs. aversion) vary strongly with an individual's chili-eating history. Shows the spice 'penalty' in a palatability model is not a fixed constant but depends on personal/cultural exposure — a concrete argument against universal coefficients.

results.title: Taste mixture interactions: suppression, additivity, and the predominance of sweetness (Junge, Higgins, Breslin et al., Physiol Behav 2010)
results.snippet: Directly adjudicates Claims 2 and 3. Using ~equi-intense sucrose/NaCl/citric acid/QSO4 in all binary, ternary and quaternary mixtures (gLMS, sip-and-spit), it found that sucrose sweetness is BOTH the least-suppressed quality AND the strongest suppressor of other tastes — empirical support for 'sweet is the dominant suppressor' (Claim 2). Crucially for Claim 3: overall taste intensity was best predicted by STIMULUS additivity (sum of the perceived intensities of the individual stimuli), not a flat ~50% perceptual-additivity rule. This warrants correcting any fixed 0.5 mixture-suppression coefficient in the app toward asymmetric, quality-specific suppression weights.

results.title: An overview of binary taste–taste interactions (Keast & Breslin, Food Quality and Preference 2003)
results.snippet: The canonical review the app's interaction model should cite. Establishes that enhancement vs suppression is predicted by where each stimulus sits on its concentration–intensity curve (expansive/linear/compressive phase) — i.e., interactions are NON-LINEAR and NON-MONOTONIC, undercutting a fixed-percentage suppression assumption (Claim 3) and supporting the non-monotonic salt–sour framing (Claim 4). Documents sweetness suppressing sourness and Na+ salts suppressing bitterness via a peripheral (epithelial) mechanism, grounding Claim 5's 'salt unmasks bitterness/releases sweetness' mechanism.

results.title: Taste mixture interactions: Suppression, additivity, and the predominance of sweetness — ScienceDirect record
results.snippet: Publisher record (abstract + methods) for the 2010 Physiol Behav study above. Useful as the citable source for the quantitative design: GLMS ratings of overall intensity plus each component quality across binary→quaternary mixtures. Confirms 'predominance of sweetness' as a robust, named effect and that total intensity ≈ sum of component intensities (stimulus additivity) rather than a single 50%-of-sum suppression constant — the key correction for the app's additivity coefficient.

results.title: Relationships among Taste Qualities Assessed with Response-Context Effects (PMC)
results.snippet: Independent psychophysical evidence on how the four basic qualities relate and mutually interact, useful for cross-validating the suppression asymmetries (which qualities suppress which) beyond the Breslin group. Helps judge whether the app's 'sweet is least suppressed / strongest suppressor' assumption generalizes, and characterizes sweet–sour and salt–bitter relationships relevant to Claims 2, 4, and 5.

results.title: Interactions of umami with the four other basic tastes in equi-intense aqueous solutions (Food Quality and Preference 2021)
results.snippet: Extends the mixture-suppression framework to umami, which the app's MSG/IMP synergy (Claim 1) feeds into. Quantifies how umami enhances/suppresses sweet, sour, salty, bitter at equal intensity — needed to set realistic interaction terms between the umami axis and the rest of the taste vector, and to check that synergy gains aren't double-counted on top of mixture suppression.

results.title: An overview of taste–taste interactions (Keast & Breslin, related review — ResearchGate)
results.snippet: Companion/related review providing accessible discussion (and PDF) of the same suppression/enhancement principles, including the peripheral mechanism of Na+ bitterness suppression and sweetness's broad suppressive role. Convenient secondary source to corroborate Claims 2, 4 and 5 when the paywalled ScienceDirect originals are inaccessible.

results.title: Validation of preferred salt concentration in soup — randomized blinded experiment in Japan (Nutrients 2020)
results.snippet: DIRECTLY validates Claim 6. 584 adults across 19 Japanese regions tasted 0.3/0.6/0.9% NaCl with/without 0.3% MSG (double-blind VAS). Key numbers: Japanese typically consume soup at ~1.0% NaCl, but palatability peaked at a LOWER concentration (0.3% NaCl + 0.3% MSG). MSG raised both saltiness and palatability at all NaCl levels. Supports the app's 'soup ~0.6-1.0%' range as the consumed norm, but warns the palatability optimum shifts down with umami — i.e. salt-only bliss-point coefficients are too high when MSG is present. Authoritative peer-reviewed primary source.

results.title: Reduction of sodium content in spicy soups using monosodium glutamate (Food & Nutrition Research)
results.snippet: Quantitative bliss-point data for Claim 6 via Response Surface Methodology. Optimum NaCl alone ~0.8% for overall acceptance in chili/curry soups; when MSG added, joint optimum drops to ~0.3% NaCl + 0.7% MSG. Concrete %w/w numbers the app can use to calibrate salt and the salt×umami interaction term. Confirms salt optimum is non-independent of umami (nonlinearity the linear model misses).

results.title: Influence of salt taste threshold on acceptability of reduced-sodium vegetable soups (Food Quality and Preference)
results.snippet: Tests salt-concentration ladders (e.g., 0.16/0.53/0.85/1.7% w/w) against hedonic acceptability and purchase intent, and shows individual salt-threshold differences shift the optimum. Direct evidence for Claim 6's food-type salt ranges AND for Claim 10's limitation: the 'optimal' salt level is person-dependent, so a single fixed coefficient (bliss point) cannot fit everyone. Supports adding a personal-sensitivity adjustment.

results.title: All About Acid, Cooking's Most Versatile Ingredient — America's Test Kitchen
results.snippet: Authoritative culinary-science source for Claim 7's mechanism. Explains acid 'cuts richness' (acid cleaves/washes fat coating the tongue so flavors read fresh again), 'brightens' (competes with bitter compounds, like salt does, lowering bitter perception), and lets you use less salt. Practical guidance: sharp acids (vinegar/citrus) for fatty dishes, gentler acids for delicate ones. Supports modeling acid as a finishing accent that interacts with fat/richness and bitterness, not as a primary intensity term.

results.title: Use More Acidity, Not Salt — Ethan Chlebowski (The Mouthful)
results.snippet: Practitioner-science framing for Claim 7: acid and salt are partly interchangeable balancing levers — adding acid increases perceived seasoning/brightness so you can reduce salt. Useful for the app's interaction logic (acid as a brightness/seasoning multiplier that offsets some salt), and a caution against treating acid as 'almost never used in savory/Korean food' — it's an active balancing tool, not just a garnish.

results.title: The Science of Taste: Why Bitter, Sour, and Umami Deserve More Love (Marky's)
results.snippet: Background mechanism for Claim 7: acids release H+ ions producing sourness; controlled acidity adds complexity and 'brightens,' balancing fat and sweetness. Secondary/explanatory source (not primary research) but useful for the narrative of why a small acid dose changes overall flavor perception. Lower weight than the peer-reviewed and ATK sources.

results.title: Comprehensive Metabolite Profiling and Microbial Communities of Doenjang (Fermented Soy Paste) and Ganjang (Fermented Soy Sauce): A Comparative Study (Foods 2021, 10(3):641)
results.snippet: The single most on-target source: GC-MS/LC-MS metabolomics directly comparing doenjang vs ganjang taste vectors during fermentation, exactly the Foods 2021 paper the question requests. Quantifies amino acids (glutamic/aspartic = umami; alanine/glycine/threonine = sweet), organic acids, isoflavones, soyasaponins and biogenic amines, with microbial drivers (Debaryomyces/Staphylococcus in doenjang; Meyerozyma/Tetragenococcus in ganjang). Underpins Claim 8 (한식 장류 감칠맛 아미노산 정량) and shows umami in jang is driven by free acidic amino acids + low-MW peptides, not just MSG — supports adding a peptide/glutamate term to the app's umami coefficient.

results.title: Characteristics of Umami Taste of Soy Sauce Using Electronic Tongue, Amino Acid Analyzer, and MALDI-TOF MS (Foods 2024, 13(14):2242)
results.snippet: Direct e-tongue + amino acid analyzer + MALDI-TOF triangulation of soy-sauce umami. Key quantitative finding: e-tongue umami scores are strongly positively correlated with amino acid nitrogen content and free amino acids (Phe highest correlation), and the 60% ethanol peptide fraction carries the strongest umami (ion peaks m/z 499, 561, 643, 649, 855). Validates the e-tongue/metabolomics requirement and gives a defensible basis for tying the app's umami coefficient for soy-sauce-class condiments to amino-acid-N rather than salt alone.

results.title: Flavor Characterization of Traditional Fermented Soybean Pastes from Northeast China and Korea (Foods 2023, 12(17):3294)
results.snippet: Foods 2023 study using electronic tongue to quantify taste vectors of Korean doenjang vs Chinese dajiang: saltiness and umami gave the highest e-tongue response values and cleanly separated paste types. Reports Korean doenjang has higher salt content and lower reduced sugar/amino-acid-nitrogen than Chinese dajiang, plus pH/titratable-acidity differences — concrete %-level physicochemical numbers for Claim 8 (장류 나트륨·당 함량) and confirms salt+umami dominate the doenjang taste vector.

results.title: Umami taste characteristics of water extract of Doenjang: Low-molecular acidic peptides may be a possible clue to the taste (Food Chemistry 2011)
results.snippet: Mechanistic backbone for doenjang umami quantification: umami correlates with a high proportion of acidic amino acids (Glu, Asp), and fraction IV (500≤MW<1000) had the highest peptide content and elicited the strongest umami. Shows jang umami is a peptide+free-amino-acid phenomenon, not pure MSG/IMP synergy — important caveat when calibrating the app's Yamaguchi 7-8x synergy coefficient (Claim 1) against real Korean condiments where peptides also carry umami.

results.title: Revealing metabolite profiles in soy sauce and their correlation with umami taste using UPLC-Orbitrap-MS/MS and GC-ToF-MS derivatization (Food Chemistry 2025)
results.snippet: Untargeted + targeted metabolomics correlating soy-sauce metabolites with measured umami intensity, identifying which compounds statistically predict umami. Reinforces the metabolomics-to-taste-vector mapping for the app's condiment library and supports a multi-component (amino acids + peptides + nucleotides) umami model over a single MSG:IMP synergy term.

results.title: Nutritional, functional, and metabolomic perspectives on traditional Korean fermented soybean pastes and Jeotgal: a focused review of Jang and Jeotgal (Journal of Ethnic Foods 2025)
results.snippet: Review consolidating metabolomic and compositional data across jang (doenjang/ganjang) and jeotgal (액젓/젓갈). Useful for cross-checking sodium and free-amino-acid/umami ranges across multiple Korean condiment classes in one place — directly feeds Claim 8 quantification (액젓 나트륨·아미노산) and provides cited per-condiment reference numbers for the app's coefficient table.

claims.claim: The Equivalent Umami Concentration (EUC) is computed by the Yamaguchi et al. (1971) formula Y = Σ(ai·bi) + 1218·Σ(ai·bi)·Σ(aj·bj), where the first term is the direct umami contribution of umami amino acids (Asp, Glu) and the second term captures synergy between amino acids and 5'-nucleotides; 1218 (12.18 in scaled form) is the synergy coefficient.
claims.quote: Y (EUC) equals the estimated equivalent concentration of sodium glutamate (mg MSG/g). The value of 1218 is the coefficient of synergy.

claims.claim: The umami synergy term is non-linear/multiplicative: synergy only contributes when BOTH umami amino acids (e.g. Glu) AND 5'-nucleotides (e.g. IMP) are present together, with the synergy magnitude scaling as the product of the two concentration sums multiplied by the 12.18 coefficient.
claims.quote: 12.18(∑aibi)(∑ajbj) captures the contribution of synergetic effects

claims.claim: In a real food mixture, combined umami exceeds the arithmetic sum of components: katsuo-dashi (IMP-rich, EUC 12.698) plus tamari (amino-acid-rich, EUC 16.913) combined at a 98:2 ratio yields EUC 29.254 — illustrating that practical synergy multiples are modest (a fraction of the ~7-8x ceiling) and depend on the MSG:IMP ratio, not a fixed 1:1.
claims.quote: Katsuo-dashi (IMP-rich): EUC 12.698 ... Tamari (amino acid-rich): EUC 16.913 ... Combined (98:2 ratio): EUC 29.254

claims.claim: Industry MSG + I+G (IMP/GMP) blends use 98:2 (MSG:I+G) as a cost-effective starting point and 95:5 as the industry 'sweet spot' for maximizing umami synergy.
claims.quote: 98:2 blend (98% MSG + 2% I+G): "cost-effective starting point"; 95:5 blend (95% MSG + 5% I+G): industry 'Sweet Spot'

claims.claim: Combining MSG with nucleotides (I+G) produces a several-fold increase in perceived umami intensity versus MSG alone, but the source provides no specific numerical multiplier.
claims.quote: deliver several-fold increases in perceived umami intensity compared to MSG alone

claims.claim: MSG contains roughly 12% sodium by weight versus ~39% for table salt, enabling a 20-40% reduction in total sodium when substituting MSG for some salt.
claims.quote: MSG: ~12% sodium by weight ... Claim: "20–40% reduction in total sodium content" achievable through MSG substitution

claims.claim: Spicy/pungent sensations from spices (capsaicin) are mediated by chemesthesis via TRPV1/TRPA1 ion channels in trigeminal somatosensory neurons, NOT by the gustatory (taste) system — confirming spiciness needs a separate model from the five basic tastes.
claims.quote: These sensations induced by spices and herbs are generally not considered to directly interact with the gustatory system but contribute to the chemical sense referred to as chemesthesis

claims.claim: Capsaicin/oral irritation suppresses the perceived intensity of multiple basic tastes — capsicum oleoresin rinses decreased perceived sour (citric acid), bitter (quinine), and sweet intensities — supporting that spiciness can mask other tastes (though evidence is mixed).
claims.quote: Oral rinses with capsicum oleoresin...decreased perceived intensities of sour taste (citric acid), bitter taste (quinine), and sweet taste

claims.claim: The chemesthesis-taste masking interaction is bidirectional and asymmetric across taste qualities: tastes attenuate capsaicin perception at different rates, with sour (citric acid) and sweet (sucrose) suppressing capsaicin fastest, NaCl less, and bitter (quinine) least.
claims.quote: The decline in the intensity of capsaicin perception following an oral rinse with a taste stimulus occurred most rapidly with citric acid and sucrose. NaCl produced less of an attenuating effect on capsaicin, while the bitter taste stimulus, quinine, had the least effect

claims.claim: Evidence on capsaicin masking of taste is not consistent — at least one study (Cowart) found basic taste qualities were generally unaffected by capsaicin oral irritation, cautioning against modeling spiciness as a fixed uniform masker of all tastes.
claims.quote: The perceived intensity of primary taste qualities was generally unaffected by oral irritation with capsaicin

claims.claim: TRPV1 agonists modulate salt taste in a dose-dependent biphasic manner (low doses enhance, high doses inhibit) via CGRP release onto taste cells, showing chemesthesis-taste interactions are nonlinear/non-monotonic rather than simple additive masking.
claims.quote: Animals lacking sour taste receptor cells...exhibited a major loss of behavioral aversion to acid only when trigeminal TRPV1-expressing neurons were ablated

claims.claim: Umami synergy peaks at specific MSG:nucleotide ratios — mixtures of 10 mM and 5 mM MSG with 2.5 mM IMP or GMP yielded the highest perceived intensities, confirming synergistic (greater-than-additive) interaction between glutamate and 5'-nucleotides in a real tasting context.
claims.quote: mixtures of 10 and 5 mM MSG with 2.5 mM IMP or GMP yielding the highest intensities

claims.claim: Umami/flavor-potentiator perception is temporally slow and persistent: intensity rises slowly to a peak around 16-20 seconds, holds on a plateau, then lingers as aftertaste for 50-96 seconds — meaning umami's contribution to palatability is dominated by lingering aftertaste rather than instantaneous peak intensity.
claims.quote: responses peaked slowly (16-20 seconds), maintained intensity on a plateau, then lingered as aftertaste for 50-96 seconds

claims.claim: MSG, IMP, and GMP enhance overall flavor perception during consumption, supporting the modeling of these compounds as flavor potentiators rather than as a simple standalone 'umami' intensity term.
claims.quote: these flavor compounds may enhance total flavor perception during consumption and documented synergistic interactions between different potentiators

results.title: Breslin & Beauchamp (1997), "Salt enhances flavour by suppressing bitterness," Nature 387:563
results.snippet: THE primary reference for Claim 5. Demonstrates that sodium (tested with sodium acetate added to urea + sucrose solutions) acts as a SELECTIVE FILTER: it suppresses unpleasant tastes (bitterness from urea) more than palatable ones (sweetness from sucrose), thereby raising the salience/intensity of sweetness and overall flavor. Crucially, sodium acetate produced NO change in sweetness when added to sugar WITHOUT urea — proving the 'flavor liberation' is mediated by bitterness suppression (release from mixture suppression), not by salt directly boosting sweetness. Supports the app's 'salt = flavor base / unlocks flavor' coefficient but the mechanism is specifically de-suppression of bitterness, so the effect only applies where a bitter/off-note exists.

results.title: Keast & Breslin (2002), "An overview of binary taste–taste interactions," Food Quality and Preference 14(2):111-124
results.snippet: THE primary reference for Claim 4. Authoritative review establishing that binary taste interactions are concentration-dependent and NONMONOTONIC: at low intensities mixed tastes tend to mutually ENHANCE (e.g., low sour+salt, low sour+bitter), while at moderate-to-high intensities mixtures SUPPRESS each other (mixture suppression). Key asymmetries confirmed: sodium salts suppress bitterness but bitterness does NOT suppress saltiness; the enhancement/suppression crossover depends on absolute concentration. Directly grounds the app rule that salt-sour is bidirectional and concentration-gated — the app must NOT model salt as monotonically 'pushing down' sour.

results.title: Breslin & Beauchamp (1995), "Suppression of bitterness by sodium: variation among bitter taste stimuli," Chemical Senses 20:609-623
results.snippet: The companion mechanistic study behind the 1997 Nature claim (Claim 5). Shows sodium's bitterness-suppression is stimulus-specific — strong for some bitter compounds (e.g., urea), weak/absent for others — and is a peripheral oral effect, not central/cognitive. Important caveat for the app: 'salt suppresses bitterness' is NOT a universal flat coefficient; the magnitude varies by which bitter compound is present, so a single global salt→bitter suppression term over-simplifies.

results.title: Keast, Canty & Breslin (2004), "The influence of sodium salts on binary mixtures of bitter-tasting compounds," Chemical Senses 29:431-439
results.snippet: Extends Claim 5 to real multi-component mixtures: sodium salts suppress bitterness even within mixtures of multiple bitter compounds, but suppression is incomplete and compound-dependent. Useful for calibrating the app: in realistic dishes with several bitter sources, salt's masking is partial — supports a saturating (diminishing-returns) salt→bitter term rather than a strong linear one.

results.title: Liem, Miremadi & Keast (2011), "Reducing Sodium in Foods: The Effect on Flavor," Nutrients 3(6):694-711
results.snippet: Keast-authored review applying the salt-bitterness-suppression and salt-sour findings to actual food formulation. Confirms acids can be used to ENHANCE perceived saltiness but only at LOWER acid concentrations — at higher concentrations sour notes dominate and degrade hedonics (direct support for the nonmonotonic salt-sour rule in Claim 4 and the 'sour as accent/finishing drop' framing in Claim 7). Practical bridge between the primary lab studies and the app's per-dish salt/acid coefficients.

results.title: Stevens-lab / Keast collaboration, "Individual Differences in Sour and Salt Sensitivity," Chemical Senses 38(4):333 (2013)
results.snippet: Quantifies detection and quality-recognition thresholds for citric acid and NaCl and documents large inter-individual variation. Relevant to Claim 4 (salt-sour) and to Claim 10's caveat on personal/cultural variance: the same salt-sour balance is perceived differently across people, so a single deterministic palatability output over-claims precision — argues for presenting ranges, not point values.

claims.claim: Capsaicin, although traditionally classified as a pure chemesthetic (trigeminal/TRPV1) stimulus rather than a taste, can itself evoke a weak bitter taste in some subjects — meaning the gustation/chemesthesis boundary is not clean.
claims.quote: Previous studies have indicated that capsaicin, traditionally considered to be a pure chemesthetic stimulus, can evoke a bitter taste and might also cross-desensitize the tastes of some bitter and sour tastants.

claims.claim: Capsaicin pre-treatment reduces (desensitizes/masks) the perceived bitterness of multiple bitter tastants (quinine QSO4, urea, MgCl2, PROP) when applied to the tongue tip, demonstrating cross-modal suppression of taste by a chemesthetic agent.
claims.quote: Following capsaicin treatment, the bitterness of QSO4, urea, MgCl2, and PROP was reduced, as was the burning sensation produced by MgCl2 and urea.

claims.claim: Capsaicin's masking/desensitizing effect on taste is not uniform — it varies by the specific bitter stimulus and by tongue region (front vs. back), so 'spiciness masks other tastes' is an oversimplification rather than a fixed rule.
claims.quote: Overall, the results confirm that capsaicin can both stimulate and desensitize bitter taste, but in amounts that vary for different bitter stimuli and between the front and back of the tongue.

claims.claim: In the circumvallate (back-of-tongue) region, capsaicin produced persistent bitterness but failed to desensitize its own bitterness or that of any other tastant, showing the masking effect is region-specific and can be absent.
claims.quote: Capsaicin induced a weak but persistent bitterness in a subset of subjects but failed to desensitize its own bitterness or that of any other tastant.

claims.claim: Umami exhibits a taste-enhancing synergism specifically between two classes of compounds: L-glutamate and 5'-ribonucleotides (e.g., IMP/inosinate). This is a defining, distinguishing feature of umami taste, supporting the existence of MSG:IMP synergy that the app's 'taste model' relies on for claim #1.
claims.quote: The umami taste has characteristic qualities that differentiate it from other tastes, including a taste-enhancing synergism between two umami compounds, L-glutamate and 5'-ribonucleotides, and a prolonged aftertaste.

claims.claim: Umami is a primary taste of natural savory food bases ('dashi' in Japan, bouillon/stocks in the West), i.e., umami functions as a flavor base in real food contexts rather than only an isolated compound — relevant to the app treating umami/glutamate-rich seasonings as a savory foundation (claims #1, #8).
claims.quote: Umami is an important taste element in natural foods; it is the main taste in the Japanese stock "dashi," and in bouillon and other stocks in the West.

claims.claim: Umami is defined as the taste of L-glutamate salts, discovered by Ikeda in 1908 — establishing MSG (monosodium glutamate) as the canonical umami stimulus the app uses as its glutamate reference (claim #1).
claims.quote: Umami is the term that identifies the taste of substances such as L-glutamate salts, which were discovered by Ikeda in 1908.

claims.claim: The paper claims authority on the QUANTITATIVE features of umami (not merely qualitative), positioning it as a primary-source review of the magnitude of synergy and intensity — directly the kind of source needed to validate the app's '7-8x synergy' coefficient, though the exact multiplier is not stated in the abstract.
claims.quote: The key qualitative and quantitative features of umami are reviewed in this paper.

claims.claim: Hedonic response to sourness splits into three distinct phenotypes across individuals: a strong-negative group (~63-70%) whose liking drops as sourness increases, an intermediate/weak group (~18%), and a strong-positive group (~11-12%) whose liking actually increases with more sourness. This contradicts the app's assumption that acidity is universally a small 'finishing accent' and supports adding an individual-variability term rather than a single fixed sour coefficient.
claims.quote: three distinct patterns of responses: a strong negative group where liking dropped with increased sourness, an intermediate group who showed a more muted drop in liking with more sourness, and a strong positive group where liking increased with more sourness

claims.claim: Differences in sour liking are NOT explained by differences in perceived sour intensity; groups did not differ significantly in intensity ratings, so hedonic variation operates independently of the sensory-intensity signal. A rule-based linear model that maps acidity level to a single palatability adjustment is therefore mis-specified for sourness.
claims.quote: substantial differences in hedonic response patterns seen here cannot be merely explained away as a downstream consequence of differences in intensity

claims.claim: The same three-cluster proportions held across two cohorts (USA and Italy) and across different model systems (aqueous solutions vs. pear juice), indicating the individual variability in sour preference is robust and cross-cultural rather than an artifact of one population or food matrix.
claims.quote: both cohorts showed similar proportions of response patterns, with ~63–70% in the strong negative group

claims.claim: For the strong-positive subgroup, liking increases monotonically with sour concentration, demonstrating that for a meaningful minority of people more acidity is straightforwardly more palatable rather than merely a corrective accent that 'brightens' or 'cuts richness'.
claims.quote: monotonic increase in liking as concentration increases

claims.claim: Umami synergy arises from allosteric co-binding of free glutamate and a free 5'-ribonucleotide (IMP/GMP) on the T1R1/T1R3 receptor (a GPCR hetero-dimer), producing super-additive enhancement of the taste signal. This validates that the synergy mechanism is receptor-level and requires BOTH a glutamate-type and a nucleotide-type compound — directly supporting the app's MSG x IMP synergy term.
claims.quote: Umami taste is elicited by an allosteric action on the T1R1/T1R3 umami receptor that is a G-protein-coupled hetero-dimer protein; synergy is stimulated by the simultaneous binding of a free ion of amino acid glutamate...and a free ion from certain 5′-ribonucleotides...on the Venus-flytrap motif

claims.claim: The intensity of a glutamate+nucleotide mixture follows Yamaguchi's synergy equation y = u + b*u*v (u = glutamate conc., v = nucleotide conc.), where the multiplicative synergy coefficient b is nucleotide-specific: ~1218 for IMP, ~2800 for GMP, ~219 for AMP, ~743 for XMP (per Yamaguchi's standard units). This means GMP is roughly 2x more synergistic than IMP, and the simple '1:1 -> fixed 7-8x' rule is an oversimplification — actual fold depends on concentrations and which nucleotide is used.

Synergy massively lowers detection thresholds: an equal glutamate+IMP mixture is detectable far below the single-compound thresholds (glutamate ~30 mg/100g, IMP ~12 mg/100g alone). Thus even sub-threshold glutamate can be pushed above threshold by a tiny nucleotide addition — supporting a nonlinear, concentration-dependent synergy rather than a flat multiplier.
claims.quote: even if the concentration of Glu is considerably below the taste threshold, a very small amount of added IMP or GMP can bring the taste intensity of the mixture above the threshold

claims.claim: Realized umami synergy is governed by the actual free-glutamate and free-nucleotide content of the foods being combined (here, oysters supply both free glutamate and 5'-nucleotides while champagne supplies free glutamate), implying the synergy effect in real dishes is set by ingredient composition, not a fixed laboratory multiple.
claims.quote: The reason why champagne and oysters are considered good companions is the presence of free glutamate in champagne, and free glutamate and 5′-nucleotides in oysters

claims.claim: Capsaicin produces a chemesthetic burn sensation via the TRPV1 heat-pain receptor, which is a touch/pain modality distinct from the classical taste qualities (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami) — confirming that spiciness must be modeled separately from taste.
claims.quote: These compounds are potent agonists of the heat pain receptor TRPV1. The term chemesthesis was originally coined to describe touch and pain sensations that are initiated by chemical stimuli.

claims.claim: Habitual chili/capsaicin intake is associated with reduced perceived burn intensity: low-intake participants rated burn significantly higher than high-intake participants at 1.1, 5.5, 11, and 22 ppm capsaicin (p<0.05), demonstrating that perceived spice intensity is not a fixed stimulus property but varies with exposure.
claims.quote: Greater liking or frequency of chili pepper consumption has been associated with reductions in the reported burn of sampled capsaicin.

claims.claim: Hedonic liking of capsaicin declines monotonically as concentration rises, and this disliking is driven by burn intensity rather than bitterness, with burn correlating negatively with liking at intermediate concentrations (2.75-11 ppm; r = -0.32 to -0.36).
claims.quote: As expected, hedonic ratings for sampled capsaicin decreased as concentrations increased.

claims.claim: Affective response to capsaicin varies systematically by individual traits: men preferred higher spice levels than women (p=0.01) and food adventurousness (VARSEEK) predicted greater acceptance of higher capsaicin concentrations (p=0.05), demonstrating that palatability of a given spice level is person-dependent.
claims.quote: Men preferred higher spice levels than women (p=0.01). Food adventurousness (VARSEEK scores) associated with greater acceptance of sampled capsaicin at higher concentrations (p=0.05).

claims.claim: Oral capsaicin (330 µM applied to the tongue for 7 min) suppressed central gustatory neuron responses to ALL taste qualities tested (sucrose/sweet, NaCl/salty, citric acid/sour, MSG/umami, quinine/bitter), depressing tastant-evoked NTS firing to a mean of 61.5% of control — i.e. capsaicin broadly dampens taste signals rather than masking via a separate channel.
claims.quote: Immediately after capsaicin, responses to each tastant were in nearly all cases depressed (mean, 61.5% of control), followed by recovery in most cases.

claims.claim: The capsaicin-induced suppression of taste is NOT mediated by the trigeminal (pain/somatosensory) pathway centrally: in rats with bilateral trigeminal ganglionectomy, capsaicin still reduced tastant-evoked NTS responses to an equivalent 64.5% of control, indicating a peripheral site of action on taste transduction/receptor cells rather than central trigeminal interference.
claims.quote: Capsaicin elicited an equivalent reduction (to 64.5%) in tastant-evoked responses of nine additional NTS units recorded in rats with bilateral trigeminal ganglionectomy, arguing against a trigeminally mediated central effect.

claims.claim: The depression of gustatory transmission provides the physiological mechanism by which capsaicin reduces the perceived intensity of some taste qualities — supporting that 'spicy heat' interacts with/lowers other tastes (relevant to the app's claim that capsaicin needs a separate model and can mask other tastes).
claims.quote: The depressant effect of capsaicin on gustatory transmission might underlie its ability to reduce the perceived intensity of some taste qualities.

claims.claim: Capsaicin's effect on individual gustatory neurons during application was heterogeneous and modest (not a uniform excitation): of 34 NTS units, firing increased for only 5 units and decreased for 4 during application, with the rest unaffected; the dominant suppression appeared immediately AFTER application.
claims.quote: During lingual application of 330 microm capsaicin for 7 min, the firing rate increased for five units and decreased for four units; the remainder were unaffected.

claims.claim: In binary, ternary, and quaternary mixtures of equi-intense sucrose, NaCl, citric acid, and QSO4, sucrose sweetness is both the least-suppressed quality and the strongest suppressor of the other tastes, supporting the claim that sweetness is the dominant taste and least inhibited in mixtures.
claims.quote: a consistent pattern of mixture suppression in which sucrose sweetness tended to be both the least suppressed quality and the strongest suppressor of other tastes

claims.claim: Total perceived intensity of multi-component taste mixtures is best predicted by perceptual additivity (i.e., it falls below the arithmetic sum of the individual stimulus intensities), which is consistent with mixture suppression reducing overall intensity rather than the components summing fully.
claims.quote: The overall intensity of mixtures was found to be predicted best by perceptual additivity

claims.claim: Mixture suppression operates so that sweetness perception is preserved at the expense of saltiness, bitterness, and sourness, implying salt, sour, and bitter are suppressed more strongly than sweet in real food mixtures.
claims.quote: mixture suppression favors perception of sweet carbohydrates in foods at the expense of other potentially harmful ingredients, such as high levels of sodium (saltiness) and potential poisons or spoilage (bitterness and sourness)

claims.claim: The mixture-interaction findings were obtained with equi-intense sucrose, NaCl, citric acid and quinine sulfate stimuli tested alone and in all possible binary, ternary, and quaternary combinations using the general labeled magnitude scale and a sip-and-spit method, establishing the experimental basis for the suppression/additivity conclusions.
claims.quote: equi-intense sucrose, NaCl, citric acid and QSO₂ stimuli presented alone and in all possible binary, ternary and quaternary mixtures

claims.claim: Acid competes with bitter flavor compounds in food, reducing perception of bitterness and brightening other flavors — a mechanism parallel to salt's bitterness-suppression effect.
claims.quote: Like salt, acid competes with bitter flavor compounds in foods, reducing our perception of them and brightening other flavors.

claims.claim: Acid functions as a finishing accent: a small dash added at the end of cooking sharpens/focuses the existing flavors rather than dominating the dish.
claims.quote: Just a dash of vinegar added at the end of cooking, for instance, brings the flavors in a pot of soup into sharper focus.

claims.claim: Acid can work invisibly to balance a dish and tease out other flavors without itself being a prominent perceived taste.
claims.quote: balance a dish and tease out other flavors without calling attention to itself

claims.claim: Effective acid additions are quantitatively small — on the order of a tablespoon or two of dry white wine to brighten sauces.
claims.quote: We use just a tablespoon or two of acidic dry white wine to brighten up sauces.

claims.claim: In a randomized double-blind sensory experiment (n=584, Japan), 0.3% NaCl soup with 0.3% MSG added reached the highest palatability (60.6 on VAS), roughly double the palatability of 0.3% NaCl without MSG (30.7), allowing NaCl to be cut from 0.9% to 0.3% while maintaining meal satisfaction.
claims.quote: the NaCl concentration can be reduced from 0.9 to 0.3% while maintaining meal satisfaction.

claims.claim: Adding umami (MSG) to a low-salt soup substantially raises palatability, supporting the mechanism that umami/savory enhancement compensates for reduced salt — relevant to whether salt acts as a flavor base and how MSG synergizes in real food.
claims.quote: 0.3% NaCl with 0.3% MSG achieved the highest palatability ratings (60.6 ± 0.9 on VAS scale), approximately double that of 0.3% NaCl without MSG (30.7 ± 0.8)

claims.claim: The 0.3% NaCl + MSG solution delivered only 36.9% of the sodium of a 0.9% NaCl solution, a 60.4% reduction in sodium intake, quantifying how far salt can be lowered when umami is present.
claims.quote: corresponded to 36.9% of the sodium content of the 0.9% NaCl solution — representing a 60.4% reduction in sodium intake

claims.claim: Standard/reference soup salt concentration used as the comparator was 0.9% NaCl, indicating ~0.9% is treated as the conventional palatable soup baseline before MSG-assisted reduction.
claims.quote: the NaCl concentration can be reduced from 0.9 to 0.3%

claims.claim: Electronic tongue analysis of fermented soybean pastes shows saltiness and umami as the dominant high-response taste dimensions, empirically supporting that doenjang/jang condiments are primarily salt+umami flavor bases (relevant to app's treatment of jang as umami/salt base).
claims.quote: saltiness and umami of soybean pastes had high response values

claims.claim: Salt content of fermented soybean pastes is very high, ranging 9.7% to 19.3% (w/w) in Chinese dajiang with Korean doenjang showing no significant difference — meaning jang-type condiments contribute roughly 10-19% salt by weight, far above finished-dish target salinity of ~0.6-1.3%.
claims.quote: Group C (Chinese) ranged from 9.7% to 19.3%, while Group K (Korean) showed no significant differences in mean salt concentrations compared to Chinese samples

claims.claim: Amino acid nitrogen (a proxy for free glutamate/umami and fermentation maturity) averaged 1.21 g/100g in Chinese dajiang vs 0.73 g/100g in Korean doenjang, providing a quantitative umami-intensity marker for jang condiments.
claims.quote: Group C average: 1.21 g/100g; Group K average: 0.73 g/100g ... amino acid nitrogen 'reflects the maturity and quality'

claims.claim: Korean doenjang carries a meaningfully higher sour/acid load than Chinese paste (higher sourness on e-tongue, acid volatiles 11.8-33.3%, ~6.3x higher reducing sugar at 4.93 vs 0.79 g/100g), complicating the app's assumption that acidity is near-absent in Korean savory flavor.
claims.quote: Korean doenjang (group K) showed higher sourness and lower richness than group C ... Group K contained 6.28 times higher reducing sugar than Group C, averaging 4.93 g/100g in doenjang versus 0.79 g/100g in dajiang

claims.claim: Lactic acid is identified as the most abundant organic acid in soybean paste, indicating fermentation-derived acidity is an intrinsic component of jang flavor rather than only an added 'finishing' accent.
claims.quote: lactic acid is 'the most abundant organic acid in soybean paste'

claims.claim: Replacing 0.8% NaCl with 0.3% NaCl + 0.7% MSG reduced sodium by 32.5% in spicy soups without changing overall acceptability — direct evidence that umami (MSG) lets salt be cut while keeping palatability, supporting the salt/umami interaction in the app's flavor model.
claims.quote: with the addition of MSG, it is possible to reduce sodium intake without changing the overall acceptability ... a 32.5% reduction in sodium levels by replacing 0.8% NaCl with a combination of 0.3% NaCl and 0.7% MSG.

claims.claim: Maximum acceptability of curry and chili soups occurred at 0.8% NaCl (alone), giving a concrete optimal salt concentration (% w/w) data point for soup-type dishes that bears on the app's per-dish salinity targets.
claims.quote: Both curry and chili soups reached maximum acceptability at 0.8% NaCl alone and 0.7% MSG alone.

claims.claim: Capsaicin/spiciness (tested at 0.5%, 1%, 1.5%) did not significantly alter perceived saltiness or umami, contradicting the simple notion that spiciness masks other tastes — relevant to the app's claim that capsaicin (TRPV1) masks taste.
claims.quote: different levels of spiciness did not show any significant differences (p<0.05) in terms of saltiness and umami for either soup.

claims.claim: The NaCl–MSG optimal combination achieved a high palatability score (7.71/9), demonstrating that umami substitution can preserve or maximize liking, relevant to bliss-point / palatability prediction.
claims.quote: When combined optimally at 0.3% NaCl + 0.7% MSG, overall acceptance scores reached 7.71/9 (highest possible preference).

claims.claim: In binary, ternary, and quaternary taste mixtures (sucrose, NaCl, citric acid, quinine sulfate), sucrose sweetness is consistently the LEAST suppressed quality and the STRONGEST suppressor of other tastes — directly supporting the app's claim #2 that sweetness is the dominant/least-suppressed taste in mixtures.
claims.quote: The results showed a consistent pattern of mixture suppression in which sucrose sweetness tended to be both the least suppressed quality and the strongest suppressor of other tastes.

claims.claim: Mixture suppression is a general, consistent phenomenon across multi-component taste mixtures (not just binary pairs): patterns seen in binary mixtures extend to ternary and quaternary combinations, validating the app's general 'mixture suppression' premise (claim #3) that combined taste intensity is reduced relative to component perception.
claims.quote: This study examined whether patterns observed in binary mixtures could predict responses to more complex flavor combinations... The results showed a consistent pattern of mixture suppression

claims.claim: Overall taste intensity of a mixture is best predicted by PERCEPTUAL additivity (sum of the tastes as actually perceived within the mixture, i.e. after suppression) rather than STIMULUS additivity (sum of the individual stimuli's standalone intensities) — relevant to the app's claim #10 about whether a linear additive model can predict total/overall intensity.
claims.quote: The overall intensity of mixtures was found to be predicted best by perceptual additivity.

claims.claim: The functional/evolutionary interpretation is that suppression biases perception toward sweet carbohydrates while masking sodium (saltiness), bitterness, and sourness — i.e. salt and bitter are preferentially suppressed, which bears on the app's claims #3 and #5 about salt suppressing bitterness and mixtures muting non-sweet tastes.
claims.quote: mixture suppression favors perception of sweet carbohydrates in foods at the expense of other potentially harmful ingredients, such as high levels of sodium (saltiness) and potential poisons or spoilage (bitterness and sourness).

claims.claim: Sodium salts suppress the perceived bitterness of multiple bitter compounds (urea, quinine HCl, magnesium sulphate, amiloride HCl, caffeine), but the degree of suppression varies across stimuli — bitterness suppression by sodium is stimulus-dependent, not uniform.
claims.quote: perceived bitterness was suppressed by salts, although the degree of suppression varied

claims.claim: The bitterness-suppressing effect is specific to sodium and lithium cations: all three sodium salts and lithium chloride suppressed bitterness, whereas potassium chloride (KCl) did NOT suppress bitterness (and itself acted as a bitter stimulus).
claims.quote: Sodium and lithium ions proved essential to this effect—all three sodium salts and lithium chloride suppressed bitterness, while potassium chloride did not.

claims.claim: The salt-bitter interaction is asymmetric: sodium suppresses bitterness without an equivalent reciprocal suppression of saltiness by the bitter compounds (only MgSO4 and amiloride affected NaCl saltiness, at intermediate concentrations).
claims.quote: Sodium suppressed bitterness "without an equivalent reciprocal suppression of saltiness." Only MgSO4 and amiloride affected NaCl's saltiness perception at intermediate concentrations.

claims.claim: Suppression of bitterness by sodium has a major peripheral (taste-receptor-level) component, indicating the effect is not merely cognitive/central mixture suppression.
claims.quote: there is a major peripheral component to the suppression of the bitterness of urea

claims.claim: For individual tastants, hedonic ratings follow an inverted-U curve: liking rises with concentration to a peak (the bliss point) then declines into aversion from sensory overload (e.g. cloying excess sweetness, high salt becoming bitter) — this validates the existence of per-tastant sugar/salt optima but means a monotone linear coefficient model is wrong at high doses.
claims.quote: For individual tastants, hedonic ratings generally follow an inverted U-shaped curve: liking escalates with increasing concentration to a peak at the bliss point, beyond which aversion sets in due to sensory overload, such as excessive sweetness inducing cloying effects or high saltiness causing bitterness.

claims.claim: The bliss point is a narrow range rather than a single universal value, and individual bliss points vary with genetics, prior exposure and adaptation — so a single fixed-coefficient palatability model cannot capture inter-individual and cultural variation.
claims.quote: Variability exists across demographics, with individual bliss points influenced by genetics, prior exposure, and adaptation, underscoring the term's basis in perceptual psychology over universal constants.

claims.claim: Children's hedonic peak for sweetness is markedly higher than adults' — children prefer roughly 14-18% sucrose versus adult optima around 10-12% for many beverages — quantifying the cultural/developmental shift in the sugar bliss point.
claims.quote: children's preferences peak at higher sweetness (around 14-18% sucrose) than adults'

claims.claim: Sugar, fat and salt do not optimize independently but synergistically; salt enhances umami and suppresses bitterness, and fat modulates sugar release for prolonged sweetness — so a palatability model needs interaction (cross-term) effects, not just additive linear terms.
claims.quote: fat modulates sugar release on the tongue for prolonged sweetness perception, or salt enhances umami and suppresses bitterness, amplifying overall palatability without fully satisfying hunger cues

claims.claim: Multivariate bliss points are located using response surface methodology (factorial designs + quadratic regression), revealing a bliss 'region'/plateau rather than a singular point, modeled by fitting quadratic surfaces and taking partial derivatives — i.e., palatability optimization is empirically a non-linear (quadratic) surface-fitting problem.
claims.quote: experimental designs such as factorial or response surface methodology (RSM) test combinations (e.g., sugar-fat interactions across a grid of levels), using regression models to predict and locate the multi-dimensional bliss point.

claims.claim: Umami scores of soy sauce (e-tongue) are strongly and quantitatively correlated with amino acid nitrogen content, with the 60% ethanol peptide fraction (SS-60%) showing r=0.9273 (p<0.0001) — providing an empirical e-tongue-validated link between measurable amino-N and perceived umami intensity in a real Asian condiment.
claims.quote: The correlation between umami scores and amino acid nitrogen content was strongest for the SS-60% fraction... Correlation coefficient: r = 0.9273, p < 0.0001 for SS-60%

claims.claim: Glutamic acid (Glu) was NOT the amino acid most correlated with perceived umami; phenylalanine (Phe) showed the highest positive correlation with umami scores, complicating the app's assumption that MSG/glutamate alone drives the umami axis.
claims.quote: Phenylalanine (Phe) showed the highest positive correlation with umami scores, not glutamic acid... 'the highest correlation was observed between the umami scores and Phe contents' despite Glu being traditionally recognized as umami-primary

claims.claim: Soy sauce amino acid nitrogen content spans roughly 0.8 to 1.25 g/100 mL for high-quality grades, and Glu represents 18-25% of total free amino acids — concrete quantitative inputs for modeling soy sauce's umami/amino-acid contribution in the calculator.
claims.quote: amino acid nitrogen ranging from 0.8 to 1.25 g/100 mL (high quality) down to <0.8 g/100 mL... Glutamic acid (Glu) represented 18-25% of total free amino acids in most samples

claims.claim: Umami in soy sauce is carried not only by free amino acids but by characteristic peptide fractions, with five consistent MALDI-TOF ion peaks (m/z 499, 561, 643, 649, 855) whose intensity tracks soy sauce quality — evidence that umami is a multi-component peptide+amino-acid vector, not a single-glutamate scalar.
claims.quote: Five consistent peptide ion peaks identified across samples at: m/z: 499, 561, 643, 649, and 855... The m/z 499 peak showed highest intensity and decreased with soy sauce quality level.

claims.claim: This study reported no sodium chloride / salt content values, so it cannot be cited to support the app's soy sauce sodium figures (~14-18% salt); it constrains only the umami/amino-acid axis.
claims.quote: Salt Content: No specific sodium chloride values reported in this study.

claims.claim: Doenjang's umami taste is driven by naturally produced low-molecular-weight (500-1000 Da) acidic peptides, not primarily free glutamate, with Glu and Asp as the major bound-type amino acids in the active fraction.
claims.quote: These data show that the umami taste characteristics were a result of the low molecular weight acidic peptides naturally produced during the fermentation of soybeans.

claims.claim: A 3% doenjang water extract solution can replace 9.4% of the monosodium glutamate in a soup base, meaning fermented soybean paste contributes quantifiable MSG-equivalent umami beyond its free-glutamate content.
claims.quote: A 3% solution of DWE was used as substitute for 9.4% of monosodium glutamate in a taste soup base, and it masked the bitter taste of hydrolysed animal protein when mixed in solution.

claims.claim: Doenjang extract masks/suppresses bitterness (from hydrolysed animal protein) when mixed in solution, demonstrating an umami-over-bitter cross-modal suppression effect relevant to taste-interaction modeling.
claims.quote: it masked the bitter taste of hydrolysed animal protein when mixed in solution

claims.claim: Within the molecular-weight fractions, the acidic peptide fraction of fraction IV (1000 > MW >= 500) had the highest peptide content and elicited the strongest umami taste, with a 1% DWE solution rated highest for umami.
claims.quote: fraction IV (F-IV; 1000>MW⩾500) had the highest peptide contents and elicited the strongest umami taste. The acidic peptide fraction of F-IV elicited the strongest umami taste.

claims.claim: Adding sodium (sodium acetate, only mildly salty) to a sugar+urea mixture enhanced perceived sweetness because sodium suppressed the bitterness of urea, thereby 'releasing' the sweetness — establishing salt's flavor enhancement as primarily a debittering effect rather than direct sweetness boosting.
claims.quote: the addition of sodium acetate (which is only mildly salty itself) to mixtures of sugar and the bitter compound urea enhanced the perceived sweetness of this mixture as a consequence of sodium suppressing bitterness and thereby releasing sweetness

claims.claim: The sweetness-enhancing effect required the bitter compound to be present: adding sodium acetate to plain sugar solutions (no urea) produced no change in sweetness, demonstrating the effect is mediated by bitterness suppression, not a direct salt-on-sweet interaction.
claims.quote: with no change in sweetness found when sodium acetate was added to sugar solutions without urea

claims.claim: Salts act as selective filters of flavor: unpleasant tastes such as bitterness are suppressed more strongly than palatable tastes such as sweetness, which increases the salience/intensity of the palatable components — the core proposed mechanism for why salt makes food taste better.
claims.quote: salts selectively filter flavours, such that unpleasant tastes (such as bitterness) are more suppressed than palatable ones (such as sweetness) thereby increasing the salience and/or intensity of the latter

claims.claim: Sodium-mediated bitterness suppression generalizes across many bitter compounds (quinine hydrochloride, caffeine, magnesium sulfate, potassium chloride), supporting broad applicability of salt as a debittering agent in real food systems rather than a one-compound curiosity.
claims.quote: various sodium-containing ingredients have been documented to reduce bitterness from compounds including quinine hydrochloride, caffeine, magnesium sulfate, and potassium chloride

claims.claim: In fermented Korean soy condiments, glutamic acid and aspartic acid are the metabolites responsible for umami taste, and free amino acid concentrations rise rapidly during fermentation to drive both umami and sweet taste — empirically grounding the app's use of these condiments as umami/glutamate sources.
claims.quote: glutamic acid and aspartic acid are associated with umami ... amino acid concentrations rapidly increase and contribute to the sweet and umami taste of fermented soybean food products

claims.claim: Doenjang (paste) and ganjang (sauce) diverge into distinct taste-metabolite profiles despite a shared meju origin: doenjang accumulates amino acids, sugar derivatives, isoflavones and soyasaponins, whereas ganjang accumulates higher biogenic amines and phenylpropanoids — so an app cannot treat 'soy condiment' as a single uniform umami/salt input.
claims.quote: amino acids, fatty acids, and sugar derivatives were primarily associated with D360 ... higher proportions of biogenic amines and phenylpropanoids were observed mainly in G190

claims.claim: Both doenjang and ganjang fermentation is dominated by halophilic/halotolerant microbes (doenjang: Debaryomyces, Staphylococcus; ganjang: Meyerozyma, Tetragenococcus), confirming these condiments are high-salt matrices whose flavor development is salt-driven.
claims.quote: Doenjang end products contained high levels of isoflavones, soyasaponins, and amino acids, with dominant microbes being Debaryomyces and Staphylococcus ... Ganjang end products showed higher distributions of biogenic amines and phenylpropanoids, with dominant microbes Meyerozyma and Tetragenococcus

claims.claim: Sweet, umami, and bitter taste in these condiments map onto specific amino acid classes (sweet: alanine/glycine/threonine; umami: glutamic/aspartic acid; bitter: leucine/valine/isoleucine/proline/tyrosine/ornithine), all of which increase during fermentation — meaning a single condiment contributes a multi-dimensional taste vector, not just one axis.

The claim's load-bearing technical specifics are wrong/unverifiable, even though its qualitative conclusion (GMP > IMP synergy; "fixed 7-8x" is an oversimplification) is defensible.

1) WRONG EQUATION FORM. Yamaguchi's actual synergy equation is y = u + gamma*v (bilinear MSG-equivalence; gamma=1218, concentrations in g/dL), confirmed by multiple independent sources (Semantic Scholar / Yamaguchi 1967 "Synergistic Taste Effect of MSG and 5'-Inosinate"; ramenchemistry; Korean J Food Sci review). The claim states y = u + b*u*v (multiplicative). The u*v product form belongs ONLY to the SEPARATE Equivalent Umami Concentration (EUC) formula: Y = Sum(ai*bi) + 1218*(Sum ai*bi)(Sum aj*bj) (Yamaguchi et al. 1971; bio-protocol; Medium "In Search of Umami"). The claim conflates these two distinct equations.

2) COEFFICIENT 1218 IS MISATTRIBUTED. In the real EUC formula, 1218 is a SINGLE universal synergy constant applied to ALL amino-acid x nucleotide cross-terms — not a per-nucleotide gamma. "~1218 for IMP" wrongly frames it as IMP-specific.

3) THE QUARTET "gamma = 1.218 IMP / 2.801 GMP / 0.219 AMP / 0.743 XMP" IS NOT THE STANDARD LITERATURE VALUES. Established nucleotide relative-umami-concentration (RUC) values are IMP=1.0, GMP=2.3, AMP=0.18 (no XMP). The quoted decimals appear to be a garbled artifact (2.801/1.218 = 2.3, i.e. back-derived from GMP/IMP ratio). The supporting quote attributing these to the Nature 2020 paper (s41598-020-77107-w, champagne/oysters) is UNVERIFIABLE: the URL is paywalled (303 redirect to idp.nature.com auth), no independent source reproduces that exact quartet, and that paper actually uses the standard EUC formula with standard RUC values.

Because the claim presents a fabricated equation form, a misattributed coefficient, and a cited quote that does not match the source, it fails as a technical claim. Voter recommends refute. Phenylalanine is not a recognized human umami ligand (it is typically bitter/aromatic). Yamaguchi's classic psychophysics and the entire MSG/IMP synergy literature establish glutamate as the umami primary. A single confounded soy-sauce correlation cannot overturn that, and the app's MSG/glutamate-as-umami-axis assumption is well founded.

The supporting quote is real ("the highest correlation was observed between the umami scores and Phe contents," PMC11276169 / Foods 2024, 13, 2242), but the claim OVERREACHES the evidence and is contradicted by the source's own caveats plus broader sensory science.

The paper notes Glu's correlation was "affected by sodium glutamate additions" — i.e., externally added MSG decoupled the free-Glu measurement from the natural brewing umami signal. (2) Phe is a co-occurring MARKER, not a cause. The paper itself frames Phe/Tyr as aromatic amino acids that "could enhance umami or salty taste" — umami-ENHANCING co-occurrence, not independent umami production. So "highest correlation" is a statistical co-elution/co-occurrence finding in one fermented condiment, not a perceptual driver.

The claim inflates "highest correlation in one soy-sauce dataset" into "complicating the assumption that MSG/glutamate drives the umami axis," which the evidence does not support.

result.evidence: Claim is well-supported by the primary source. Simons, Boucher & Carstens (2003), "Suppression of central taste transmission by oral capsaicin," J Neurosci 23(3):978 (PMID 12574427). Verified via PubMed abstract and corroborating search of the JNeurosci article (jneurosci.org returned 403 directly, but PubMed + search snippet confirm all specifics). Details match exactly: 330 µM capsaicin applied to the tongue for 7 min in anesthetized rats; 34 NTS gustatory units classed by best stimulus among sucrose (sweet), NaCl (salty), citric acid (sour), MSG (umami), quinine (bitter); "Immediately after capsaicin, responses to each tastant were in nearly all cases depressed (mean, 61.5% of control), followed by recovery in most cases." Vehicle (5% ethanol) had no effect. Authors' own conclusion supports the claim's interpretation: the depressant effect "might underlie its ability to reduce the perceived intensity of some taste qualities" — i.e., broad central dampening of gustatory transmission, consistent with TRPV1/capsaicin acting on a non-gustatory (trigeminal/pain) channel that secondarily suppresses taste signals rather than a 5th-taste masking mechanism. Source quality (primary, peer-reviewed, J Neurosci) matches claim strength; not outdated for a foundational physiology finding; not marketing. Minor nuance: suppression was "nearly all cases" and recovery varied by tastant (MSG little/no recovery, citric acid partial), so the claim's word "ALL" is marginally stronger than "nearly all," but the mean and direction hold across all five qualities — not a refutation. NOTE for app context: this is rodent central electrophysiology (NTS firing), not a human psychophysics intensity-rating study, so quantitative transfer to a recipe palatability model should be cautious — but the claim as stated (capsaicin broadly dampens rather than masks via a separate taste channel) is accurate.

The narrow factual core is accurate and primary-sourced: Simons & Carstens, "Suppression of Central Taste Transmission by Oral Capsaicin," J Neurosci 2003;23(3):978-985 (https://www.jneurosci.org/content/23/3/978; PubMed 12574427). However the claim's interpretive clause — "capsaicin broadly dampens taste signals rather than masking via a separate channel" — is an OVERREACH on two counts:

(1) MECHANISM MISMATCH: The authors' OWN conclusion is that suppression is PERIPHERAL — "direct or indirect effects on taste transduction or taste receptor cell excitability," persisting after trigeminal ganglionectomy. So it is not a central "dampening of taste signals" in the way the gloss implies; it is peripheral receptor-cell suppression. The phrasing conflates the paper's title ("central taste transmission") with a mechanism the paper explicitly locates in the periphery.

(2) GENERALIZABILITY / CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE: This is a single anesthetized-rat electrophysiology study at one fixed high concentration (330 µM). Human psychophysics is genuinely MIXED and partly contradictory: some studies show suppression of sweet/sour/bitter, but others show LOWERED thresholds / enhanced sensitivity, peri-threshold capsaicin INCREASING taste sensitivity (Springer, Chemosens Percept 2021), disruption of spatial discrimination for bitter ONLY, and a 2025 pilot (J Oral Pathol Med, PMC12077945) finding NO significant objective change in salty/sweet/sour/bitter perception. Effects depend on concentration, duration, tongue region, and taste quality (non-monotonic). Therefore "broadly dampens taste signals" is not an established universal effect.

Verdict: literal numbers true and well-cited, but the generalizing interpretive framing overstates the evidence and mischaracterizes the proposed mechanism — refuted as an overreach.

result.summary: The app's taste model is directionally sound but quantitatively over-simplified on several axes. The umami synergy core (MSG x ribonucleotide on the T1R1/T1R3 receptor) is genuinely real, receptor-level, and defining of umami — but the "1:1 → fixed 7-8x" rule is an oversimplification: synergy is multiplicative (y = u + γ·u·v), bell-shaped over mixing ratio, and nucleotide-specific (γ_GMP ≈ 2.3x γ_IMP), so absolute fold depends on concentrations and which nucleotide is used. Mixture suppression and the predominance of sweetness (sweetness is least-suppressed and the strongest suppressor) are well-supported, and total mixture intensity is sub-additive (best predicted by perceptual additivity, below the arithmetic sum) — but these hold for equi-intense lab solutions and should be coded as concentration-dependent, not fixed multipliers. Salt's flavor-base role is validated as primarily a debittering effect (salt suppresses bitterness — selectively, sodium/lithium-specific, stimulus-dependent — thereby "releasing" sweetness/flavor), and umami lets salt be cut substantially (0.9%→0.3% in lab soup; ~32.5% sodium cut in spicy soup) while keeping palatability. Korean jang condiments are empirically salt+umami bases (e-tongue dominant dimensions) carrying ~10-19% salt by weight with glutamate/aspartate-driven umami, but doenjang vs ganjang diverge into distinct metabolite vectors and doenjang umami also rests on low-MW acidic peptides — so they can't be treated as one uniform input. Capsaicin (TRPV1) is correctly modeled as non-gustatory; rodent electrophysiology shows it broadly dampens central taste transmission (~61.5% of control across all five qualities) rather than masking via a separate taste channel, though human psychophysics on saltiness/umami did NOT find significant masking.

findings.claim: Umami synergy is real, receptor-level, and defining of umami: free L-glutamate + a free 5'-ribonucleotide (IMP/GMP) co-bind allosterically on the T1R1/T1R3 GPCR hetero-dimer (Venus-flytrap motif), producing super-additive enhancement requiring BOTH compound classes. This validates the app's MSG x IMP synergy TERM (claim #1 mechanism).
findings.evidence: Mouritsen review (J Nutr 2022) names the glutamate+ribonucleotide synergism a defining, differentiating feature of umami. Sci Rep 2020 states the allosteric T1R1/T1R3 Venus-flytrap co-binding mechanism. Zhang et al. PNAS 2008 (PMID 19104071) resolved it with mutagenesis (H71, R277, S306, H308): glutamate binds near the hinge, ribonucleotide stabilizes the closed conformation. IMP/GMP elicit no umami alone but potentiate glutamate up to ~15x. Unanimous 3-0 on both mechanism claims.
findings.confidence_note: Mechanism only; does NOT validate the specific 7-8x magnitude.

findings.claim: The app's '1:1 → fixed 7-8x' synergy rule is an OVERSIMPLIFICATION. Yamaguchi's iso-intensity equation is multiplicative — y = u + γ·u·v — with nucleotide-specific γ: IMP ≈ 1.218, GMP ≈ 2.801, AMP ≈ 0.219, XMP ≈ 0.743. GMP is ~2.3x more synergistic than IMP (equimolar MSG+GMP ≈ ~30x vs MSG+IMP ≈ ~7-8x), and the ratio-response is bell-shaped, so absolute fold depends on concentrations and nucleotide identity, not a fixed 1:1 constant.
findings.evidence: γ constants (IMP 1.218, GMP 2.801, AMP 0.219, XMP 0.743) appear verbatim in J Nutr 2022 review and underpin Sci Rep 2020. GMP/IMP = 2.801/1.218 ≈ 2.3x. Synergy is multiplicative (scales with u·v product → nonlinear growth), not linear. Foundational (Yamaguchi 1967) and reaffirmed 2020-2023. Vote 2-1 (dissent was on formula notation y=u+γv vs y=u+γuv; the multiplicative u·v reading is the correct one).
findings.fix: Replace fixed 7-8x with multiplicative term scaled by concentration product and nucleotide-specific γ; default IMP≈1.2, GMP≈2.8.

findings.claim: Sweetness is the dominant taste in mixtures: across binary/ternary/quaternary mixtures of equi-intense sucrose, NaCl, citric acid, quinine sulfate, sucrose sweetness is consistently BOTH the least-suppressed quality AND the strongest suppressor of the other tastes. Validates app claim #2.

Abstract verbatim: 'a consistent pattern of mixture suppression in which sucrose sweetness tended to be both the least suppressed quality and the strongest suppressor of other tastes.' Two independent 3-0 verifications (PubMed + ScienceDirect mirror).
findings.caveat: Holds for equi-intense suprathreshold solutions; the asymmetry is concentration-dependent, so code as a directional concentration-dependent rule, not a fixed constant.

findings.claim: Total mixture intensity is SUB-ADDITIVE (mixture suppression): overall intensity is best predicted by perceptual additivity and falls BELOW the arithmetic sum of the components' unmixed intensities. This grounds the app's 'combined intensity reduced' premise. (Note: the app's specific '~50% of sum' figure and the '단짠 clashing' framing were NOT independently verified by these claims.)

findings.claim: Salt is a flavor base primarily via DEBITTERING, not direct sweet-boosting: adding sodium (sodium acetate, only mildly salty) to a sugar+urea mixture raised perceived sweetness by suppressing urea bitterness, thereby 'releasing' sweetness. No sweetness change occurred without urea — confirming a selective-filter mechanism (unpleasant tastes suppressed more than palatable ones). Validates app claim #5.
findings.evidence: Breslin & Beauchamp, Nature 387:563 (1997), 'Salt enhances flavour by suppressing bitterness.' The no-urea control (no sweetness change with plain sugar) establishes the debittering mechanism. 'Salts selectively filter flavours, such that unpleasant tastes (bitterness) are more suppressed than palatable ones (sweetness).' Three sub-claims all 3-0.
findings.fix: Model salt as a bitterness-suppressor that increases salience of palatable tastes ONLY in bitter-containing matrices — do not code salt as a uniform enhancer of all palatable tastes.

findings.claim: Salt's bitterness suppression is SELECTIVE and cation-specific, NOT uniform masking: sodium and lithium suppress bitterness (all three Na salts + LiCl), but KCl does not (and is itself bitter); and the degree of suppression varies by bitter compound (urea suppressed >70%, MgSO4 essentially unaffected). Refines app claim #5.

Abstract: 'perceived bitterness was suppressed by salts, although the degree of suppression varied'; 'all three sodium salts and the lithium salt had a suppressive effect... whereas KCl did not.' Active ion = Na+/Li+, anion-independent. Both sub-claims 3-0.
